questions.q: What table does a Flow live on, and what is its basic structure?
options: sys_hub_flow; exactly one Trigger followed by an ordered sequence of Actions
wf_workflow; a graphical canvas of connected activities
sys_hub_action_type_definition; a single configurable step
sysapproval_approver; a chain of approval records
questions.explain: Every Flow is a sys_hub_flow record, structurally reducing to one Trigger plus an ordered sequence of Actions.

questions.q: What record type defines an Action and gives it its configurable inputs in the Flow Designer step picker?
options: sys_hub_flow
wf_workflow
sys_hub_action_type_definition
sys_trigger
questions.explain: An Action's definition — built-in or custom — is a sys_hub_action_type_definition record, which is what populates the step picker with configurable inputs.

questions.q: What's the real structural difference between a Flow and a Subflow?
options: A Subflow lives on a completely different table than a Flow
Both are sys_hub_flow records, but a Subflow is flagged as a subflow type and is designed to be called by other flows rather than triggered directly
A Subflow cannot contain any Actions
A Flow can only contain one Action, while a Subflow can contain many
questions.explain: A Subflow is still a sys_hub_flow record, just flagged as a subflow type with its own defined inputs/outputs, meant to be called by other flows rather than triggered directly.

questions.q: Why does this course wait until Chapter 3 to teach building custom Actions?
options: Custom Actions involve real scripting and are a deeper skill worth their own dedicated chapter
Custom Actions don't actually exist in Flow Designer
Built-in Actions can never be used in a flow with a custom Action
Flow Designer only supports one Action per flow
questions.explain: Custom Actions are a real skill involving scripting, which is why this course gives them a full chapter later rather than covering them in Lesson 2.

questions.q: In the example flow described in this lesson — Incident created, set a field, call a shared notification Subflow, log the outcome — what does that example actually illustrate?
options: That flows can only ever contain built-in Actions
That a Subflow must always run before any Action in a flow
That one Flow record can combine a Trigger with built-in Actions, custom Actions, and a Subflow call together
That Triggers are optional on a Flow
questions.explain: The example shows all three building blocks working together inside one Flow: a Record trigger, Actions, and a call to a reusable Subflow.
